title: How to evaluate whether a financial advisor is worth the cost
description: The math of the 1% AUM fee vs. the value of behavioral coaching.
content:
The standard fee for a financial advisor is 1% of Assets Under Management (AUM). If you have a $1 Million portfolio, you pay $10,000 every year, regardless of whether the market goes up or down. Over 30 years, this fee can consume 25-30% of your total potential wealth. Is it worth it? For some people with complex lives, yes. For others with simple W-2 income, it is highway robbery. This guide provides a framework to audit your advisor's value.

Key Takeaways

  • The Cost of 1%: A 1% fee reduces your safe withdrawal rate in retirement from 4% to 3%. That is a massive reduction in lifestyle.
  • Value Add: Advisors earn their fee through Tax Planning, Estate Planning, and Behavioral Coaching (preventing panic selling). They rarely earn it through 'Stock Picking.'
  • Fee-Only vs. AUM: The modern trend is 'Flat Fee' or 'Hourly' advice. Paying $3,000/year flat is often cheaper than 1% of a growing portfolio.
  • Fiduciary Standard: Never hire a non-fiduciary. They are salespeople allowed to sell you expensive products for a commission.

Why It Matters (US Context)

The barrier to calling yourself a 'Financial Advisor' in the US is low. Many are insurance salesmen in disguise. Look for the **CFP® (Certified Financial Planner)** designation. It is the gold standard for education and ethics.

The 'Hurdle Rate' of Advice

To justify a 1% fee, an advisor must generate >1% in extra value (Alpha) compared to a Vanguard Index Fund. Where does that value come from?

1. Investment Selection (Value: ~0%)

Most advisors just put you in a diversified portfolio of funds. You can do this yourself with a 3-Fund Portfolio or Target Date Fund. There is zero value here.

2. Financial Planning (Value: High)

Running simulations: "Can I retire at 55?" "How do I fund the trust for my disabled child?" "Roth Conversion strategy?" This is real work requiring expertise.

3. Behavioral Coaching (Value: Massive but Rare)

Vanguard's 'Advisor Alpha' study suggests coaching adds 1.5% in value by stopping you from selling at the bottom of a crash. If your advisor talked you off the ledge in 2020 or 2008, they earned their fee for a decade.

When to Hire vs. DIY

  1. Stage 1: The Accumulator (<$500k, W-2 Job).
    Verdict: DIY or Robo. You don't need a human. Your tax situation is simple. Just buy index funds.
  2. Stage 2: The Complex Life ($500k - $2M, Business Owner, Divorce).
    Verdict: Hourly Planner. Pay a CFP $2,000 for a comprehensive plan, then execute it yourself.
  3. Stage 3: The Delegator ($2M+, Aging).
    Verdict: AUM Advisor. At this stage, you might want someone to manage it so your spouse is protected if you pass away. The 1% fee is a convenience tax you can afford.
  4. The Audit Question: Ask your advisor: "Can you show me the total fees I paid last year in dollars, including fund expense ratios?" If they hesitate, fire them.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is a 'Fee-Only' advisor?

They are paid ONLY by you (Client). They receive $0 commissions from selling funds or insurance. This removes conflict of interest. Always choose Fee-Only.

Is 1% standard?

Yes, but negotiable. For portfolios >$1M, you should push for 0.75% or 0.50%. Never pay 1% on a $5M portfolio.

Can I fire my advisor?

Yes. It's easy. Open an account at Fidelity/Vanguard and request an 'ACATS Transfer'. They pull the assets over. You don't even have to talk to your old advisor.
